#3295. ‘Yellowstone’ Meets ‘Desperate Housewives’ in Netflix’s Ambitious 2-Season Thriller

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Of all the things Sophie O’Neil (Brittany Snow) could have packed for her first night out in East Texas, the one that might have spared her a great deal of trouble was a sanitary pad. When a stranger asks her for one in the bathroom at an NRA fundraiser, Sophie offers a tampon, the stranger declines, and the two discover something they can agree on in Sophie’s purse. By the time they’ve each taken a Xanax, Sophie has made her first friend in Maple Brook. She’s also about to discover that the woman who just got half undressed in front of her is the wife of her husband’s boss.

There are any number of places The Hunting Wives could have introduced Margo Banks (Malin Åkerman), including the stage where she joins her oil tycoon husband, Jed (Dermot Mulroney), as he floats the idea of running for governor. Having Sophie meet her in the bathroom first is considerably more fun. Everybody else at the party sees a prospective first lady of Texas. Sophie gets to spend the rest of the evening looking at that woman and thinking about what the two of them just did. Anybody who spent eight seasons of Desperate Housewives waiting for company to arrive at Bree Van de Kamp’s house at the worst possible moment should feel right at home. Adapted by Rebecca Cutter from May Cobb’s novel, The Hunting Wives has an eight-episode first season on Netflix and a second arriving on Thanksgiving Day, November 26. That gives you a perfectly respectable excuse to spend the long weekend with the Banks family, provided you’re prepared to explain what’s happening on the television when a relative wanders in.

John Dutton would understand Jed Banks just fine. One man made his name in Montana cattle country and the other made his in Texas oil, but both have spent enough time being the most important man in the room to figure they might as well be governor. What gives The Hunting Wives its own angle on familiar Yellowstone territory is where it sends Sophie once Jed finishes talking. Margo wants to know what she thought of his speech. Imagine being new in town, having exactly one professional connection through your husband, and discovering that his boss’s wife would like a little constructive criticism.

A look around Margo’s friend group explains how much is riding on her liking the answer. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) is married to the sheriff. Jill (Katie Lowes) is the pastor’s wife, and her son Brad (George Ferrier) is the local basketball star. Between them, these women have Sunday morning, Friday night, and any trouble you might get into in between pretty well covered. Most jealous friends have to settle for scrolling back to the beginning of your Instagram. When Callie catches on to Margo’s interest in Sophie, she has the resources of the sheriff’s office at her disposal.

Jill, meanwhile, can be perfectly sweet to Brad’s girlfriend, Abby (Madison Wolfe), while making it clear she thinks her son could do better. Lowes gets at something wonderfully aggravating about a mother who has promoted herself to the third person in a teenage relationship. You can imagine how Jill would describe the encounter to Brad afterward, and how ridiculous Abby would sound trying to explain what his mother did wrong. That’s where the Wisteria Lane resemblance runs deepest. Half the pleasure of watching these women misbehave comes from knowing whose side the neighbors would take if anybody complained.

Snow is funny in the early going because Sophie seems to share the audience’s judgment about everything happening around her, right up until Margo asks if she’d like to come along. There’s a lovely bit of cowardice in how long Sophie can pass off her interest as good manners. Going to the fundraiser was Graham’s idea, after all. Dinner with the Bankses could conceivably fall under the heading of supporting her husband’s career. Buying a pistol and leaving it at Margo’s place because Graham wouldn’t approve takes a little more explaining.

Åkerman makes Margo’s attention feel as good as Sophie thinks it does, even when we have an excellent view of the woman who was getting that attention yesterday. Early on, Margo offers Sophie a ride home from a bar, leaving a visibly disappointed Callie behind. You could spend the whole ride anticipating what might happen between the two women in the car, or you could spend it dying to get back to the bar to hear what Callie has to say. Even the woman who didn’t get invited along has a scene you want to see.

There is, of course, a murder to solve. The Hunting Wives opens with a girl running for her life before taking us back three weeks, and what makes those eight episodes go down so easily is how often you can forget about the shooting altogether. Jed and Margo have Sophie and Graham over for dinner, the hosts have rather different ideas about what’s on offer than their guests do, and suddenly the most pressing question in East Texas is how on earth these people are going to face each other at work on Monday.

#3294. How Often You Need to Order From Amazon to Make Prime Worth It

Black Friday isn't until Nov. 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sales have been ramping up for several days. For frequent Amazon shoppers, Prime can quickly pay for itself—mostly thanks to the free shipping perk. But how does the math shake out if you aren't regularly ordering from Amazon? Is it worth signing up if you only shop during major sales?

Millions of Amazon Prime users currently pay $14.99 per month or $139 per year for their memberships—though other plans cost less if you qualify. For example, the Amazon Prime Student program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

If you’re on the fence about signing up for (or renewing) your Prime membership, here’s how to judge whether or not the benefits outweigh the $139 cost.

Here are the main perks of Amazon Prime that make it worth the cost for so many users.

Free two-day shipping on millions of items: This is the main draw of Prime. If you shop frequently on Amazon and want quick free delivery, the shipping perks alone may make Prime worthwhile. Prime members also get free same-day delivery on over 3 million items in eligible areas. The ultra-fast (and morally suspect) shipping usually costs $9.99 per order for non-members, though you can choose lower-cost or free shipping options if you're willing to place larger orders and wait longer to receive them.

Access to Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals. If you ask me, the content library isn’t as robust as Netflix or Hulu, but this is still an added value.

Other Prime benefits: You also get Amazon Music for streaming songs, Prime Reading for ebooks, magazines, and audiobooks; Prime gaming, free photo storage, and occasional exclusive discounts/deals.

Amazon Prime Rewards Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon/Whole Foods purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the annual fee.

Number of users: Prime benefits can be shared with other members of your household. The more users, the more value per person.

Let's say you don't care about Prime Video, Amazon Music, or free e-books, and just want to know if you'll save money you would otherwise be spending on shipping.

For non-Prime members, Amazon requires a minimum order of $35 to qualify for free shipping on eligible items. The average shipping costs for non-members aren't publicly listed, and can vary by item and shipping speed, typically ranging from $5 to $10.

For our purposes, I messed around on my non-shared, non-Prime Amazon account to find an average shipping cost of around $6 per order (assuming the order total fell below the $35 threshold, of course). Of course, shipping costs will vary depending on the item and how quickly you want it, but let’s compare the cost to the appeal of Prime’s two-day shipping option. So, we have the cost of individual online orders (around six bucks) compared to the free delivery that comes with an $139 annual fee. This means the costs you’d save on shipping alone make Prime worth the cost as long as you place more than two dozen orders in a year.

In other words: The $139 annual fee pays for itself as long as you order from Amazon Prime at least twice a month.

Of course, this conclusion is strictly in terms of shipping costs. How it stacks up ethically is between you and the person in the mirror.

And then there's this important caveat: You can still get free shipping from Amazon without a Prime membership, provided your order has $35 or more of eligible items. However, this won't grant you Prime shipping speed—your order will typically take five to eight days to be delivered. But you can place fewer, larger orders and wait a little longer, and still never pay for shipping.

Also worth considering is how much of that membership cost you'll be able to recoup via exclusive Prime Day offers. During the sale, some items will be heavily discounted only for Prime members—but whether the Prime Day price is really a "deal" will vary greatly based on the item you're buying. Some of those "big discounts" aren't any greater than what the item typically sells for. The Prime Day price can even be higher than other sale prices throughout the year. That's why it's important to make sure what you're ordering is something you planned to buy anyway—and that the sale price is actually a true bargain—before you order.

The cost of a Prime membership is a solid value for anyone using Amazon 23 times per year or more—especially if you're also watching shows on Prime Video or purchasing something that is deeply discounted for Prime Day. But if you only shop on Amazon a few times a year and don't take advantage of Prime Day offers or the other benefits, then that $139 annual fee isn't necessarily paying for itself.

Of course, if you are interested in Prime Day bargains, you can always sign up right before the start of the sale and then cancel your membership after Prime Day is over—but Amazon doesn't always make it easy on you.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

#3288. 9 Books From the 2010s That Are Officially Classics Today

What makes a book a classic? It's a text that has stood the test of time for at least a few years and has proven to be substantially influential and widely celebrated over time. It's a text that attained cultural and artistic relevance and maintains it as the years pass; it's historically relevant, universally significant, and worthy of being counted among history's "greats." Thankfully for those who love modern literature, there are a handful of 2010s books that are officially classics today.

Of course, artistic appreciation is and always will be an almost entirely subjective matter, but looking back at the biggest classics from the 2010s, it's almost undeniable that they still hold the elements that make up a classic book: historical relevance, cultural impact, and artistic merit without equal. From non-fiction masterpieces like The Warmth of Other Suns to speculative fiction cornerstones like The Way of Kings, these are books that definitely live up to the hype.

No conversation about 2010s literature could possibly be complete without getting into non-fiction, which was absolutely massive (both commercially and culturally) throughout the whole decade. The biggest masterpiece that the genre produced was Isabel Wilkerson's The Warmth of Other Suns, which traces the decades-long Great Migration of nearly six million Black Americans fleeing the Jim Crow South for Northern and Western cities between the 1910s and 1970s.

It took Wilkerson 15 years of extensive research to complete The Warmth of Other Suns, and the result ended up being one of the best American book masterpieces of the 21st century. It's a towering work of non-fiction art that reads like a sweeping novel, anchoring its research in the deeply personal biographies of three real individuals. It was modern classics like this that sparked the non-fiction boom of the 2010s.

Before it became one of the best Irish TV series of the 21st century, Normal People was a romance drama novel by Sally Rooney. A massive bestseller and winner of several awards, it's one of the most perfectly written books of the 21st century, about two young Irish teenagers from vastly different social backgrounds who navigate an intense, on-and-off romantic bond from high school through university.

The coming-of-age genre produced several great romance novels over the course of the 2010s, but it's hard to point to one that had more of a substantial pop-cultural impact than Rooney's sophomore novel. Normal People captures the emotional, social, and economic anxieties of the millennial generation through a story of such profound thematic and emotional power that just about anyone should be able to appreciate it, no matter their age.

In Madeline Miller's Circe, an overlooked nymph banished to a remote island masters witchcraft and carves out her own destiny amid gods and mortal heroes. It's an unforgettable retelling of the story of one of Greek mythology's most iconic characters (mostly framed as a reimagining of Homer's Odyssey), and it's absolutely worth reading even for people who don't typically have much interest in mythology-inspired fantasy books.

The 2010s gave us several fantasy books that are perfect masterpieces, but few quite as exceptional or popular as Circe. Miller took a character that had long been seen as a villainous seductress and flipped the narrative altogether, exploring Circe's interiority in a way far too complex to catalog the book as one of those typical "misunderstood villain" narratives that plagued the 2010s. The prose is beautiful, the character writing is powerful, and the book was so popular that it sparked a whole new wave of feminist mythological retellings.

Far and away one of the best books of the 2010s, the Nigerian novel Americanah came as part of a major boom in popularity and cultural relevance that African literature saw throughout the 2010s. It follows two young Nigerian lovers, whose paths diverge across the United States and the United Kingdom as they're forced to navigate race, class, and cultural identity abroad before they can reunite in a changed Nigeria.

Books about the immigrant and diasporic experiences became far more prevalent and popular during the 2010s, and few masterpieces demonstrate the quality of such writing better than Americanah. Written with a perfect balance between razor-sharp wit and sweeping narrative scope, it's a brilliant redefinition of traditional immigrant stories and one of the most sincere love stories that 2010s literature ever told. If there's any African novel that's today an official classic, it's surely this one.

The subgenres of high, epic, and heroic fantasy have also delivered many an incredible masterpiece throughout the 21st century so far, and the 2010s were certainly no exception. The decade saw the bulk of the output of Brandon Sanderson, who has quickly become one of the most prolific speculative fiction authors currently working. Case in point: The Way of Kings, about a brutal war of vengeance on a storm-ravaged world where ancient magic is fading.

Far and away one of Sanderson's best books, this first chapter in The Stormlight Archive is arguably also the author's novel that is most worthy of being considered a modern classic. Tremendously vast in scope, ambitious in plotting and worldbuilding, and emotionally resonant in its psychologically profound character work, The Stormlight Archive is undeniable evidence of the unmatched power of epic high fantasy.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Further proof of how ingrained in the mainstream books about marginalized experiences became throughout the 2010s is the success of author and journalist Min Jin Lee's epic historical fiction novel Pachinko, which just so happens to be one of many great books recommended by Barack Obama. In it, a young Korean woman pregnant by a married man marries a gentle minister and moves to Japan, sparking a four-generation saga of survival and resilience.

Before Pachinko, few readers outside East Asia knew about the Zainichi, ethnic Koreans living in Japan during and after Japanese colonial rule who were subjected to systemic discrimination for generations. But far from just serving as a learning experience, reading Pachinko is also a journey elevated by the incredible moral complexity and psychological depth with which Min Jin Lee writes.

Back in 1992, Donna Tartt wrote The Secret History, easily one of the best and most impactful debut novels of the '90s. The reception for her second novel, 2002's The Little Friend, was significantly more mixed. Nine years later came her third novel, the Pulitzer-winning The Goldfinch, and it may just be Tartt's magnum opus. In it, a teenage boy steals a priceless painting as he navigates the grief of surviving a terrorist bombing that killed his mother.

It's one of the best books published since 2010, an absolute masterclass in modern Dickensian storytelling that, at nearly 800 pages in length, somehow manages to not have a single page of fluff or wasted space. Combining energetic thriller plotting with profound meditations on loss, obsession, and the redemptive power of art, Tartt delivered one of the defining masterpieces of 21st-century English-language literature.

N. K. Jemisin's Broken Earth trilogy made history by becoming the first book trilogy ever to have each installment win the Hugo Award for Best Novel in consecutive years. But as great as books two and three are, this is one of those book series that peaked with their first entry: The Fifth Season, a science fantasy masterpiece about a mother journeying across an apocalyptic supercontinent to rescue her kidnapped daughter as the world tears itself apart around her.

Speculative fiction delivered so many of the 2010s' greatest masterpieces that it deserves immense amounts of credit, and there is arguably no speculative fiction book from the decade more fit to be called a modern classic than The Fifth Season. Boldly experimental and daring in its structure and creative elements (including some chapters written in the second person), it's a visceral allegory of oppression that has somehow only gotten timelier and more potent with age.

Upon publication in 2012, Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl revolutionized modern thriller writing, reshaping both publishing trends and narrative tropes across the domestic thriller subgenre in particular. In it, after Nick Dunne's wife vanishes on their fifth wedding anniversary, mounting evidence and a media circus turn him into the primary suspect in the investigation. The narrative that comes from such a premise makes for the single biggest, most official modern classic of the 2010s.

One of those mystery books that are a masterclass in prose, Gone Girl is not only an enrapturing thriller baked into layers upon layers of suspense and subtext, but also an intelligent dissection of modern marriage and media sensationalism. It's cool, tense, timely, subversive, and it pushed a new wave of domestic noir fiction whose influence can still be felt to this day. If there's any modern classic from the 2010s that's an absolute must-read, it's this one.

#3287. I Tried Building My Own Interactive World in Google Genie, but Real-Time AI Engines Aren't There Yet

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Beyond the Gemini assistant, Gemini Notebook, and various other AI offerings, Google also develops Genie, a world-building engine intended to help you create immersive visual experiences and games using only text prompts. Think of them like AI videos you can interact with and move through.

With the recently launched Genie 4 update, this tool is purportedly even more powerful. It now allows you to request live edits (like "make it snow") and incorporate sound and dialog into your prompts. Google is also promising more realistic physics and natural movements in its renderings.

These promises point to the future of AI in all kinds of ways—from robotics to world sims—but the tool requires a lot of computing power, and access is limited for the time being. You can dive in now if you're on one of the Google AI Ultra plans ($99.99 or $199.99 a month), or join the waitlist if you're a Google AI Pro user ($19.99 a month). But if you've got access, is it worth the effort (and money)? I put it to the test.

It's no exaggeration to say you can build an entire virtual world in Google Genie. It's going to be a more basic, less developed, and more chaotic world than the one in, say, GTA 6, but you can do it. Think of it like generating an AI video from a prompt, but you can then walk through the video and go as deep as you like, taking turns along the way.

Everything is rendered in real time, at a resolution of 720p and at 24 frames per second. That's not to say the engine is storing a massive 3D map in memory, however—after a minute or so, it's going to start to forget the places you've already seen. And while the basic layout will stay fixed, you might notice disappearing trees or changing colors.

Google's official line is "visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over time" in Genie 4, so it's a known limitation. The tool is presented as-is, with the intention to develop it further over time as models improve, and it's aimed at filmmakers, historians, designers, scientists, robotics engineers, and game developers. Or indeed, anyone who just wants to get lost in a world that isn't real.

Some of the demos you'll find as you step through the Genie 4 portal give you a great idea of the possibilities. There's a "Dino Field Guide" that, you guessed it, lets you wander safari-style through a prehistoric habitat. All the flora and fauna are neatly rendered, and you even get dinosaur quiz questions along the way—a nod to Genie's potential as an educational tool.

There's a "Villa Giallo" mini-game, which involves searching a haunted 1970s Italian villa and clicking on objects as you go; these objects act as clues to help you progress to the next room. I was also intrigued by a "White House: Code Red" experience that takes you into the West Wing during a "high-stakes national crisis." I couldn't quite figure out what the crisis was, but I definitely felt the highness of the stakes.

Someone's even built a "GTA 7" engine that drops you into a bright and vibrant cityscape. The slow speed and warped physics of the experience suggest Rockstar Games has nothing to worry about just yet—check out the disappearing cars and backwards-driving cops in the video above—but it's impressively detailed all the same, considering it all comes from a few text prompts.

Having checked out a few demos, I felt ready to put Genie 4 to the test myself. Eager not to infringe on any IP, I decided to generate a world where I wouldn't mind getting lost for a few minutes—somewhere I could get away from the stress of my day and enjoy some warmer weather.

I started with the prompt "Create a fully immersive, photorealistic 3D environment showing a pub in an English village in the middle of a hot and sunny day. The pub is surrounded by country lanes, old buildings, and woods, and a handful of villagers are walking around and drinking outside the pub. Use a first-person view and use a quiet background of birdsong and wind rustling in the trees."

It took a couple of minutes for my peaceful, idyllic world to be ready, and then I was immediately able to navigate through it using my keyboard and mouse. Once you're in your world, you are suggested certain prompts you can make use of, like strolling into the pub or getting the villagers to make a toast, and these worked well—evidence that your virtual world really is interactive (to a point).

Unsurprisingly, the usual AI video tells are in abundance: Everyone looks generic, the physics often go sideways, the text on signs is gibberish, and details don't remain fixed. Do a full 360-degree spin around, and you might find that not only have all the customers in the pub changed their appearance, but you're also at an entirely different pub.

The best feature is the ability to make real-time edits: I summoned both a storm and a cricket pitch with a few text prompts, though Genie decided to put a hut in the middle of the cricket pitch for some reason. I think I was most impressed by the moment when a cricketer walked past me and commented on the rain, providing hints of how this kind of tech could expand or augment games and virtual experiences in the future.

That said, even at v4 of Genie, this tech is still very much in the experimental stage, and while I can see the potential, it also shows just how difficult a task world-building is for an AI engine. Without 3D maps and proper physics engines as a foundation, you'll encounter a great deal of hastily rendered slop as you explore your environment. Even if you're a prompting pro, for the time being this is something to mess around with, rather than use in a practical way.

#3282. Tidal Is the First Streaming Platform to Ban AI Music

You have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service. If you own an iPhone and a Mac, you might be tempted by Apple Music; if you have more friends on Spotify, you may feel that's the best platform for you. But if your goal is avoiding AI music as much as humanly possible, there appears to be a new uncontested winner: Tidal.

On Tuesday, Tidal announced plans to ban AI music from its platform entirely. Starting Dec. 9, the company will begin taking steps to remove music it believes is entirely made with AI. Tidal says it thinks the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”

This isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music. Back in July, the company announced that it would start labeling songs completely made with AI, as well as remove tracks it found to be "fraudulent and deceptive." Other platforms have similar policies, or are rolling out similar features. Apple Music, for example, is working on AI labels for its app, too, and Spotify has pushed back on AI to some degree. However, this most recent move makes Tidal the first music streaming service to outright ban AI-generated music from its catalog.

Robert Anderson, Tidal's Music Lead, posted on X about the change. According to Anderson, Tidal identified 43% of the tracks it received in the last 90 days were AI-generated. Per the company's plan, Tidal will remove 29 million songs by the beginning of 2027, roughly 80,000 to 85,000 removals per day. Some 96% of Tidal's AI-generated songs have zero plays whatsoever.

I wouldn't be surprised to see other music streaming services follow suit, particularly Apple Music. Despite rolling out AI-powered features over the past couple of years, including Apple Music's AI-generated playlists, Apple has taken some stands against AI-generated material in general. The latest Apple TV intro was shot in-camera with practical effects, in an era where the company could have easily generated something with AI. If other companies plan to follow Tidal's lead here, my money's on Apple being first in line.

However, as it stands, Tidal is the only streaming service that supports this initiative. Soon enough, it'll be the sole music app you can use with near-zero ambiguity that the music you're listening to was at least mostly created by humans. (What a sentence.) Avoiding AI-generated music can be tricky, frustrating, and, frankly, exhausting. If that's important to you, Tidal might just be your new pick.

#3280. John Wayne’s 119-Minute Western Thriller 'The Searchers' Is a Start-to-Finish Masterpiece

Few movies have as long a trail of imitators and influence as 1956’s The Searchers. Based on Alan Le May’s novel of the same name, it’s a Western film from the Hollywood director most closely associated with the genre, John Ford, starring the face of the Hollywood Western, John Wayne. The movie might have been received somewhat tepidly as a stirring adventure film in its day, but it came to be seen as a foundational text for the New Hollywood school of filmmakers, casting a shadow over movies as diverse as Taxi Driver, Star Wars, and Paris, Texas. As a story of obsession, vengeance, and what it means to live in a society, it struck an uneasy chord for those directors, becoming something of an obsession in itself, and gave John Wayne possibly the darkest role he ever played, with his genial smile and rough monosyllabic manner of speaking twisted by John Ford.

As in Le May’s novel, the story is set in Texas just after the Civil War. In one of the most famous opening shots of all time, Martha Edwards (Dorothy Jordan) steps out of her front door to perceive a mysterious figure in the distance, her estranged brother-in-law, Confederate veteran Ethan (Wayne). While warmly accepted by the family, there is tension, marked by the harshness of the landscape (the movie was shot in Ford’s beloved Monument Valley, a location of nine of his films) and the impending threat of the Comanche tribe. After being guilted into working a recon mission with his mixed-race nephew Martin (Jeffrey Hunter), he returns to the homestead to see it’s been burned down, with everybody in it killed — except for Debbie (Lana Wood as a child; sister Natalie Wood as a teen), who has been kidnapped. So begins the search.

While John Wayne’s career is bigger than any one director, he had a handful of strong core collaborators that helped the actor build his identity and evolve artistically, even when part of his appeal was a salt-of-the-earth realism that didn’t suggest much in the way of artistry. John Ford, whom the actor met while working for Fox after a stint playing football at the University of Southern Carolina, was a fast friend and mentor. He let Wayne work in props and background on some silent films, like 1928’s Hangman’s House, and then gave him a decade in the world of low-rent Hollywood B-Westerns to establish himself, with the entry point being Raoul Walsh’s epic 1930 Western The Big Trail (on which he earned his name). After slumming it, Ford hired Wayne to play the Ringo Kid in his 1939 classic Stagecoach, and their names became deeply intertwined through decades of productions.

While the Ringo Kid was a youthful role, Ford was soon casting Wayne in deeper, more complex parts, while publicly dismissing the actor’s talents (even calling him “the big dummy,” according to Joseph McBride’s biography on the filmmaker). By 1949’s Cavalry Western She Wore A Yellow Ribbon, Wayne had graduated fully into older, authoritative roles, with a screen persona that was brash and beloved. When working with other directors, Wayne could play up the persona and audiences loved it. But Ford seemed to bring out other emotions, and The Searchers, a story that begins straightforwardly as a Western revenge thriller but soon becomes a study of the corrosive effects of the racism that built the West, demanded that from the actor.

As The Searchers’ narrative develops, and the movie grows into one of the best Westerns ever made, Ethan remains a mystery to his nephew Martin, who soon becomes the veteran’s sole ally in the quest to rescue Debbie. Years drag on as Martin’s sweetheart Laurie (Vera Miles) becomes engaged to another man. Leads are followed to nowhere, and the threat of the Comanche lingers on the land, with the chief Scar (Englishman Henry Brandon in redface) widely feared for his actions. Ethan’s hatred for the Comanche (and Native Americans at large) is presented casually but soon reveals itself as the primary engine of his soul, particularly in one brutal scene where he shoots out the eyes of a dead brave so his spirit is forced to “wander forever between the winds.” When he learns that Scar has taken Debbie as a wife, he announces his intention to kill her, as if to say that that has made her irredeemable in his eyes.

By presenting the hero of the film as an unapologetic and violent racist ready to kill his own kin, the movie challenges the preconception viewers might have had of John Wayne. For somebody like Martin Scorsese, whose films like Taxi Driver drew from Ethan’s racism and obsession with preserving Debbie for the characters played by Robert De Niro and Jodie Foster, that focus on harsh characters made an impact. Ethan is never outright called a racist — at the end of the day, he accomplishes his quest in his own brutal ways — but the movie makes it clear that he has the attitudes and behaviors of a man who can never truly be among a society: a time bomb and a blunt instrument to clear the way for civilization, whatever that might be.

Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end. Whether or not it sticks the landing, it's been one helluva ride, and we'll soon have room in the streaming schedule for other other shows about young people having a pretty rough go of it while just trying to survive.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, not just a show about girlfights. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami. The island was formerly home to a prestigious high school, and a bunch of students have snuck back for an ill-timed party on the last day of class. A bad idea, clearly, after the storm hits. Kraam (Papangkorn Lerkchaleampote), one of the few students who actually lives on the island, is trapped there along with a couple dozen classmates. Kraam knows the island, but Anan (Chutavuth Pattarakampol) assumes leadership while other students either take on necessary roles or fall in line. As the miniseries progresses, the new social order breaks down, even as the island's mysteries reveal themselves and things get weirder and more complex. Stream The Stranded on Netflix.

A handful of influencers get invited to a remote island, which is obviously a very good thing to agree to that will not lead to dramatic complications in any way. Behind the neon-lit party vibes, there's a cult at work and some ritualistic shenanigans with deadly consequences. Eden is more concerned with the survival horror than with some of the deeper themes and mysteries of Yellowjackets, but we're still playing with shifting power dynamics in this Spanish import. Stream Welcome to Eden on Netflix.

The premise of The Leftovers is brilliantly subdued: Around two percent of the world's population disappears without explanation, and it's enough to upend just about everything. Politics have adapted to the new normal, religions have collapsed and reformed, and families have had to make peace with the inexplicable loss of loved ones. The first season revolves around the Garvey family, led by Kevin (Justin Theroux), a sheriff whose wife (Amy Brenneman) left him to join a cult, while subsequent seasons broaden the scope to bring in other characters in other locations. It's more philosophical than Yellowjackets, and quieter, but the shows share an interest in the lingering effects of trauma, and in the stuff we get up to under threat and in the dark. Stream The Leftovers on HBO Max.

The 100 tells the story of the descendants of refugees of nuclear devastation who return to Earth from their habitat in space to encounter the remnants of humanity who have survived on Earth. Naturally, the first people sent to scope things out are the juvenile delinquents (better them than me), and they discover that three civilizations have risen up in the aftermath of the apocalypse, and they are all pretty scary (including one populated by cannibals, naturally). More sci-fi than horror, but the survivalist themes and mysteries here make it more than a decent match. The show builds an impressive mythology over the course of its run, leading to a conclusion that’s borderline metaphysical. Stream The 100 on Pluto TV or buy it from Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

A massive apocalyptic tidal wave strikes during the 10-year reunion of the graduating class of an all-girls high school. The event leaves them all trapped together (a nightmare in any event), and forced to survive while reliving old struggles and dramas. It's Yellowjackets-esque, absolutely, but also Australian and a comedy, which doesn't feel like as much of a stretch as you'd think given the over-the-top nature of that show. Stream Class of '07 on Prime Video.

A remote, charming town with some deep, dark secrets (the biggest of which, and one that it shares with Yellowjackets, is rather strongly hinted in the title), Gannibal stars Yuya Yagira as Daigo Agawa, a police officer from the big city who takes a job in the super cute (and, of course, remote) village of Kuge following some personal trouble. The perfectly charming Goto family runs the town, more or less, and welcomes Daigo and his family. It's all looking pretty great—until a mysterious man gives Daigo's daughter a severed finger as a gift, and his wife Yuki finds the words "Run Away" scrawled over a door in their new home. Just a couple of reasons why I'm more of a city person. Stream Gannibal on Disney+ and Hulu.

This latter-day plane crash narrative goes all-in on mystery and philosophy, virtually pioneering the timey-wimey reveal format that makes Yellowjackets so juicy. We kick off with flashbacks that peel back the layers of the various crash survivors before diving headfirst into warm-weather polar bears and mysterious underground bunkers and monsters made of smoke. Whether it's an uncommonly smart network show that rewards careful viewing or a load of nonsense is in the eye of the beholder—but it remains one of the most discussed and debated shows in TV history. Stream Lost on Disney+ and Hulu.

Kathryn Newton heads this surprisingly smart Lord of the Flies riff about a group of teenagers forced to create their own community after all the adults disappear and a dense new forest crops up around their small enclave, cutting them off from everything and everyone else. This one's about coming of age in a world where the usual rules are no longer in effect, and about how we're quick to reestablish an oppressive social order even when outside forces are no longer at work. Stream The Society on Netflix.

#3276. Ex-UFC Star Anthony Smith Has Domestic Violence, Terroristic Threats Charges Dropped

Anthony Smith won a massive legal victory in connection with his domestic violence case ... because the charges against him have officially been dropped.

Prosecutors dropped first-degree domestic violence, terroristic threats and first-degree false imprisonment charges against the former UFC star on Wednesday.

In a statement to TMZ, Smith says he's happy he can finally speak out after months of staying silent as his case has moved through the legal system ... but that silence should never have been mistaken for guilt or weakness.

Smith says he has experienced firsthand what allegations of wrongdoing can do to someone's career ... even before all the facts have come out.

He tells us, "Behind every headline was a real person. A father. A husband. A family. A livelihood. A life that existed long before these allegations were ever made. The emotional, financial, personal, and professional devastation caused by this experience cannot simply be erased by the dismissal of charges. There is no way to recover the time lost, undo the humiliation, or erase the pain my family has endured."

Smith laments that we now live in a society where accusations receive more attention than the ending resolution ... noting allegations make headlines; dismissals don't get the same attention.

He thanks those who stood beside him through the heinous accusations ... and who supported his family during an incredibly difficult period in their lives.

Smith ends his statements by saying he will not apologize for defending his name ... adding, "Others have had months to tell their version of my story. It is no longer theirs to tell. I will have more to say in the coming days, but for now I’m going to enjoy Thanksgiving and look forward to getting my life back."

As we reported ... Smith was arrested back in July. Prosecutors alleged that Smith threatened to kill his wife if she refused to go home with him. They claimed he then grabbed her and forced her into a vehicle.

When they arrived home, prosecutors alleged he attempted to hit his wife with his car multiple times. A protection order for his wife was issued -- and Smith was released on $500K bond.

iOS 27 includes a really clever new feature that aims to solve the awkward middle ground between cellular and Wi-Fi connectivity. Here’s how it works and how you can turn it on.

In a support document, Apple explains that Connectivity Assist uses cellular data to improve your connection when Wi-Fi is slow or unusable. Apple uses examples like your backyard or driveway, as well as “coffee shops, airports, sports venues, and everywhere in between.”

Essentially, the feature detects when your Wi-Fi connection is weak or unusable and intelligently uses cellular data to keep you connected.

One practical example I’ve noticed is when I walk out of my house and get in my car. Oftentimes, my iPhone will cling to my house’s weak Wi-Fi connection, making it hard to start playing Apple Music and queue up directions in Apple Maps.

Connectivity Assist solves that problem. My phone can now intelligently use cellular data to help that transition away from Wi-Fi. It’s one of many really nice quality-of-life improvements in iOS 27.

Another thing to be aware of is that you might use more cellular data with Connectivity Assist turned on. You can monitor your data usage via your carrier’s app or website, as well as in the Settings app on iPhone.

#3273. Five recent tech outages were not due to AI; the next round will be

Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.

That wasn’t the case, but the US Director of National Intelligence is one of a number of experts warning that we should expect AI-powered outages in the near future …

Earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other. A widespread Microsoft 365 outage occurred when two unrelated issues coincided. The next day saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. A few days later, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Many Apple services went offline later the same week, with retail stores also affected. Finally, United Airlines had its own widespread IT outage that grounded a significant number of flights.

Each had their own unrelated causes, with the White House stating that rumors of an AI-facilitated systemic attack by a hostile state were false.

However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that we should expect future tech outages as a result of attacks facilitated by AI-discovered vulnerabilities. CNBC reports him issuing the warning on CNN’s State of the Union.

The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.

You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot.

We already saw an example of this last month when a vulnerability discovered in PHP saw a significant number of websites being taken offline.

Microsoft President Brad Smith says it isn’t just a question of bad actors exploiting vulnerabilities discovered by AI, but companies rushing to patch these may inadvertently cause systems to fail, as Newsweek reports.

What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems.

Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you’re trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can’t take as much time to test what you’re changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong.

Major IT failures look set to be a routine event in the coming weeks and months.

#3269. As Apple works on AI agent features, banks are already blocking them

One of the most dramatic shifts in the AI landscape is the emergence of intelligent agents that can use iPhone and Mac apps in order to carry out tasks on our behalf.

We can already use third-party chatbots in this way, and we know Apple is working hard to turn Siri AI into an agent. However, before the company even gets the chance, banks are already blocking them, and this may be just the start …

The science fiction promise of AI has always been to be able to tell a computer what we want done and have the task carried out for us automatically. That’s starting to turn into a reality with the emergence of AI agents.

We’ve already seen Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and Muse gain agent capabilities, and Apple is expected to bring these to Siri AI at some point next year.

Earlier this month, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said that the company ultimately wants to go in this direction and may add these abilities next year. CEO John Ternus has reportedly been pushing Craig Federighi for faster software development, with specific mention of “moving beyond necessary improvements to Siri,” which seems likely to mean agentic capabilities.

Last week also saw a since-deleted Apple job listing detailing plans for autonomous AI agents.

We’ve already seen some of the ways in which this can go wrong, and we recently outlined three significant risks. Wired reports that banks are now responding to these by either blocking AI agents or warning customers that using them can be dangerous.

JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

Wells Fargo even goes as far as using capitals in its latest terms, stating that it will not be responsible for the consequences.

Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK

We can likely expect similar pushback in sectors like online shopping as companies fear high returns costs and other consequences from mistakes by AI agents.

Personally, I don’t give any AI agents access to any of my banking or other financial services, considering the risks to be too high. I don’t see my position changing any time soon.

What’s your take? Would you trust an AI agent with access to your bank accounts? If not, would Apple launching agentic capabilities for Siri AI change your view? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3267. If You Loved 'Cupertino,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

The film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

It’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

If you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a big payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

The true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3262. Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, stock up 30%

Nvidia has announced that disgraced CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated to the role, effective immediately. The company’s share price jumped more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also making significant gains.

It said that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so …

Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month. The New York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the company’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days. Things got even worse when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

That led to Huang being fired resigning on November 12.

Money over country. This is government intervention.

Despite putting the company at enormous risk and initially lying to its board of directors, there were calls in some quarters for Huang to be reinstated. He responded by saying that he would be “honored” to return if asked to do so.

The board of directors, however, said that it had no intention of inviting him back.

Nvidia’s chair Harvey Jones said: “The board does not intend to reinstate him.”

That changed today, with the company making the announcement in a press release.

Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The company’s stock price jumped by more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also up per Yahoo Finance.

Nvidia shares soared more than 30% Monday morning […] The S&P 500 (^GSPC) rose 4.5% following seven straight days of declines. #3260. The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

We’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

And focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

Digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:

When time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

Include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

Sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

SpiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

Mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

Cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

Sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

It’s also on clearance at Curry’s for £204, which is utterly bizarre, seeing as this machine only came out last year, but I’d recommend buying there if you’re fast. I’m not sure how long that sale price will last as I write this.

In the U.S., this machine is really overpriced. $699 for a Thermoblock espresso machine with no grinder is steep. For $699, you can get the Breville Barista Express or the Breville Bambino Plus with the Baratza Encore ESP grinder.

You can also get the De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $699, which has a built-in grinder, and the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini for $449 — which also has a built-in grinder.

See what I mean? You’d still have to buy a grinder separately to make the most of the ECF03. That’s an extra $200. An MSRP of around $400-$500 would have made more sense, putting the ECF03 in line with the best entry-level espresso machines, Breville Bambino Plus and Breville Bambino ($299).

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Of course, the ECF03 can make cold brew, so you wouldn’t need to purchase a separate cold brew maker or French press for cold brew, but I’m not sure this is worth the extra $200-$300 over Breville’s options. On top of that, the aforementioned De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo can make “cold brew” for the same price.

I use quotation marks because De’Longhi’s cold brew comes out warm — but I’ll get into that later.

While the ECF03 has a 58mm portafilter — closer to the specialty coffee commercial standard than Breville’s 54mm — I’m not sure that’s worth the extra $$$.

The ECF03 looks like (almost) everything Smeg makes: retro, stylish, and oh-so cool. The only machine to forgo the trademark Smeg aesthetic is the $1,599 Semi-Professional/Mini Pro/EMC02 (the many-monikered machine), which was a collaboration between Smeg and La Pavoni.

If you like the Smeg aesthetic, you’ll be pleased. If it’s not your cup of tea, you won’t be pleased. It’s as simple as that.

For a $699 machine, though, the ECF03 is a touch more plasticky than I’d like. That gorgeous white chassis? Shiny plastic. The steam wand knob also feels like plastic. If it’s not actually plastic, color me surprised, but it sure does look and feel like it.

There’s a manometer, which is a nice touch, but it doesn’t actually show the specific bar pressure of each step. I assume anything in the perforated section on the bottom right means over 9 bars, but I’d like numbers on the next iteration of this machine.

But the accessories. Oh, the accessories. They’re beautiful. The 58mm tamper is super weighty, making it feel incredibly high quality, and the 58mm portafilter is just as professional. They actually feel like weapons. This is the mark of a high-quality machine. If you unbox a $500+ espresso machine and the tamper is plastic, run. Run fast.

Naturally, you get a pressurized (dual-wall) and non-pressurized (single-wall) portafilter basket. I only used the single-wall one as I have the best grinder in the world, Mazzer Philos, so I didn’t need to resort to the help-I’ve-used-pre-ground-coffee-and-now-my-espresso-tastes-bad dual-walled portafilters.

The Smeg ECF03 makes delicious espresso. As mentioned earlier, I used the non-pressurized portafilters and fresh Ethiopian beans ground on my Mazzer Philos. I recommend you also use freshly ground coffee and the non-pressurized portafilters for the best experience. Pressurized portafilters can destroy nuance and delicate flavors in specialty coffee beans, but are fine for pre-ground coffee if that’s what you like.

To make espresso, I ground 18g of my Ethiopian coffee beans to click 25 on the Philos, which is coarser than the Fellow Espresso Series 1’s ($1,499) optimal grind size, but similar to the Breville Bambino’s ideal range of 22-25. For context, I use the same coffee beans for every single machine.

Here’s a photo of a “perfect” espresso. This extracted 35.6g in 26 seconds, which is in the “golden window” of espresso extraction.

As you can see, there’s a lovely crema on top, with a delicate, fluffy texture and a nice color to the shot. While this might not impress serious espresso enthusiasts — the shot was a little bitter at the end of the mouthful — it’s definitely fine if you are less of a hobbyist and more of an appreciator.

Overall, the espresso tastes very Italian. Strong-bodied, rich, and dark, even when using medium-roasted beans. Again, if you’re an espresso enthusiast, you might want to invest a little more in the Fellow Espresso Series 1 or Lelit Mara X3 ($1,999) — or the Smeg EMC02, which I still dream about.

As an integral part of this machine’s marketing, it’s only logical I discuss cold brew in detail. You access cold brew via the “Blue menu”, which is activated by pressing the power button while the machine is already switched on. The buttons will glow blue, meaning you’re in cold brew mode.

According to the manual, you’re supposed to use “one or two” ice cubes per cold brew, but I ignored that. I filled my cup about halfway with ice cubes, dosed 18g of medium-fine ground coffee in the non-pressurized portafilter basket, and set it to pull a double shot of cold brew. Not sure how you can get a “double shot” of cold brew, but I assume that’s just the machine’s limited button options.

The cold brew took four minutes and fifty-three seconds to fill my glass. The machine is programmed to dose a certain volume of cold brew, but I used a 12-ounce glass filled with ice, so I didn’t need the “whole” serving.

As you can see, it’s relatively dark, with a strong body. The ice cubes aren’t all melted — can you guess what that means? Yes, it actually brews cold! This is fantastic news; De’Longhi machines tend to brew lukewarm, or sometimes even actively warm cold brew (which then requires ice to make it cold).

As for the taste, this cold brew was fine. I wouldn’t throw away my Espro P7 French press, which I use to make cold brew the traditional way (16 hours at room temperature), but I also wouldn’t turn my nose up at rapid cold brew from the Smeg. I think this will do if you want a cold coffee in a pinch, but serious cold brew lovers need not apply.

While the ECF03 makes a delicious espresso, its steam wand isn’t as powerful as I’d like it to be. Don’t get me wrong, this is nowhere near as egregious as machines like the Casabrews Ultra ($349), but for $699, I’d expect at least a Bambino Plus-level wand.

I was able to get perfect microfoam, but it took a while to steam an 8oz jug — around a minute. Here’s a photo of a flat white I made on the ECF03.

As you can see, the milk texture is perfect, with smooth, almost melted-marshmallow texture. There are zero bubbles and the milk is extremely creamy. This tasted divine.

However, it’s worth noting that I’m an ex-professional barista and an espresso machine tester of almost three years. I have a lot of practice. If this is your first espresso machine, you will need to baby that steam wand. Because it’s lower pressure than the Breville Bambino/Bambino Plus, you’ll need to learn how to eke out delicate texture even when you can’t achieve the perfect vortex.

At 14.3 x 8.1 x 11.6 inches, the ECF03 isn’t the smallest, nor the largest, espresso machine I’ve tested. As it has no grinder, you’ll need a separate one, so I recommend making sure you’ve got enough to room for both the machine and its grinder before purchasing.

The water tank is at the back of the machine, so you’ll need a decent amount of upper-cupboard clearance space — at least 17 inches, I’d say.

Speaking of water tank, Smeg provides you with water hardness strips, but no water filter. If you wanted to filter your water, you’d need to buy that separately. Smeg sells these for $25 on its website, which is pretty disappointing to see considering this machine is already $699.

When you do need to descale, Smeg doesn’t sell its own descaler. I’d recommend using De’Longhi’s or Durgol’s, which are $19 for 2 bottles and $15 for 4 bottles, respectively.

Last but certainly not least — warranty. Smeg offers a 2-year warranty if purchased from the Smeg store or a 1-year warranty from another outlet. This is pretty disappointing when De’Longhi, Breville, and Ninja all offer 2-year warranties as standard — and many of their machines cost less than the ECF03.

The Smeg ECF03 is ideal for espresso beginners. If you want to feel fancier than, say, a Casabrews (and you have the money to back it up, of course), then by all means you should invest in a Smeg. The ECF03 is really easy to use, makes actually cold cold brew, and has a mostly useful manometer for pressure-watching.

Although the steam wand means you need to really pay attention during milk heating, if you’re willing to put the work in, you’ll get barista-quality coffee out of it. And I mean… just look at it! Everything Smeg makes is an aesthetic marvel, and the ECF03 is no different.

If you’re in the U.K., you’re getting a much better deal, but if you find it on sale in the U.S., I’m sure you won’t be disappointed.

Erin Bashford is a senior writer at Tom's Guide. She has a Master's in Broadcast and Digital Journalism from the University of East Anglia. She directs Tom's Guide's dedicated coffee video series, The Coffee Lab, which you can find on all social media channels. On top of her passion for coffee, she's a huge music nerd and is most often found wearing earbuds or headphones — or blasting music from her multi-room sound system. When she's not writing about lifestyle culture at Tom's Guide, she's probably reading a fantasy novel, writing a fantasy novel, playing The Sims, practising yoga, or hiking.
